newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal stays on course to hit EMU price target.
newsitem.headline: Portugal stays on course to hit EMU price target.

text.p: Portugal is on target to cut inflation to 2.5 percent this year, good enough to qualify for Economic and Monetary Union, despite a year-on-year blip in December, economists said on Thursday.

Year-on-year inflation ticked up to 3.3 percent in December, from 3.0 percent the previous month, although the 12-month rolling average, the government's yardstick, held at 3.1 percent, according to the National Statistics Institute (INE).
The government has set itself a target for average inflation of 2.25-2.5 percent for this year, which analysts say should be comfortably inside EMU ceilings.
The rolling average for 1996 was at the lower end of the government's 3.0-3.5 percent target range. Inflation averaged 4.1 percent in 1995.
"The downtrend in inflation continues and for the end of the year, the average is on target for 2.25 and 2.5 percent", said analyst Isabel Costa of Banco Finantia.
Economists see Portugal's inflation rate dropping sharply after May when meat price rises provoked by the madcow scare in early 1996 will have worked their way out of the index.

"For the opening months of the year, the year-on-year rate will remain around these levels or even slightly above, before falling significantly from April or May," said Cristina Casalinho of Banco Portugues de Investimento (BPI).

The positive inflation picture leaves room for the Bank of Portugal to reduce interest rates further even if there were doubts about whether the central bank would cut on Friday when it announces terms for the next commercial bank reserve period.
"It does not seem difficult to get to 2.5 percent inflation in 1997, if there is no external shock," said Armindo Escalda of Banco Santander de Negocios Portugal (BSNP).

Analysts said the year-on-year rise in December was explained by the fact that the month-on-month rate in the same 1995 month had actually declined. Anything less than a further decline in prices last month would automatically lead to a rise in the annual rate for statistical reasons.

Analysts said that a public sector wage accord holding salary increases to three percent, a slowing in government administered prices and the recent strength of the escudo all combined to help brake inflation.
The government decreed that prices controlled by the state should not rise more than two percent this year.
"The escudo is going to stay strong and inflation is going to tend to ease because of it," said another analyst at a leading Portuguese bank.
